alternatives.name: Use square brackets for generics
alternatives.description: Use List[int] style square bracket syntax by overloading __getitem__ on classes in typing module.
alternatives.reason_rejected: Actually adopted -- this was chosen over angle brackets (List<int>) because Python's parser cannot handle angle brackets without ambiguity with comparison operators.

alternatives.name: Angle brackets for generic types
alternatives.description: Use C++/Java-style angle brackets like List<int> for generic type parameters.
alternatives.reason_rejected: Python's parser treats < and > as comparison operators. Introducing them as brackets would require deep parser changes and create ambiguity.

alternatives.name: Decorator-based type hints
alternatives.description: Use decorators instead of annotations to specify types, e.g. @types(int, returns=str).
alternatives.reason_rejected: More verbose, less readable, and doesn't integrate with the existing PEP 3107 annotation syntax that was already in the language.

alternatives.name: Type hints as comments only
alternatives.description: Put all type information in comments rather than annotations, relying entirely on # type: comments.
alternatives.reason_rejected: Comments are not programmatically accessible at runtime. Annotations provide a structured, inspectable mechanism.

alternatives.name: Use existing annotation meaning from PEP 3107
alternatives.description: Keep annotations free-form as in PEP 3107 rather than standardizing them for type hints.
alternatives.reason_rejected: The community needed a shared vocabulary for static analysis. Free-form annotations had led to fragmented, incompatible uses.

objections.text: Type hints will make Python feel like a statically typed language and go against its dynamic nature.
Runtime performance concerns -- annotations are evaluated at function definition time, adding overhead.
